title: | Sabbath Evening Class: the Foundation of the New Will Always Be the Old

sense.text:
The foundation of the new will always be the old. Christianity’s cult leaders, a lot of these Christian pastors, focus on the New Testament as if it were a whole separate entity from the old. It is all one and the same. The Old Testament speaks of the New Testament within the prophets, and the New Testament is simply a further continuation of the old: a fulfillment of the old, but the old is not void. The pastors stay in the New Testament because they don’t understand the old, don’t know history, then call Israel the cult for dealing with the law of Moses, ‘that’s done away with.’

That is why these churches sit in the ghettos with crime and evil inside them and outside them: there is no order or law being taught in them. The pastors are starting to go back on their doctrine because Israelites in the streets have the congregations asking them where in the Bible tithing is money, and that the man is the head of the household. The churches are governmental institutions and social clubs, where the rich give their money away, listen to feel good, network and go about their business doing all kind of evil. Churches are prisons, all of them.

The verse itself: “I command thee this day to love the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments and his statutes and his judgments, that thou mayest live and multiply.” The Lord said love me, by what? By keeping my commandments.

“But if thine heart turn away, so that thou wilt not hear”: you will not listen to the Most High God, “but shalt be drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish.” Go against his laws and break his commandments and you die. You will not live, and you will lose the land he gave you, the land promised to your fathers.

“I call heaven and earth to record this day against you.” The Old Testament is a record: a record of what Israel promised to do, and what they ended up doing anyway according to that same record.

“I have set before you life and death.” Life is keeping the commandments; death is not keeping them. There is no free will in it the way Christianity means it: you do and you live, you don’t and you die. There is no ‘do what you want to do in Christ.’ Christianity says Christ died on the cross and nailed all of your responsibility to it: Christ died for you to be a rapist, a homosexual, a thief, to sell drugs, to murder, to get drunk; you ain’t got to do nothing, just believe. That’s insanity.

“Blessing and cursing” is the life and the death. Kingdom is blessing; slavery is cursing.

“Therefore choose life”: choosing life is choosing the commandments. That is the life he is talking about, “that both thou and thy seed may live.”

“That thou mayest love the Lord thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life.” God is your life, and you do what he says. He is “the length of thy days”: he prolongs your days for keeping his commandments, “that thou mayest dwell in the land which the Lord sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”

That is the point the chapter was read for: the commandments of God are life and blessing, and to denounce those ordinances, those commandments, is death and cursing. Keep in mind: the commandments of God are life.

Baruch goes here because Pastor Gino Jennings and his church subscribe to the Apocrypha, which most Christian pastors don’t acknowledge, though the whole King James Bible originally had it. So his own congregation, who come at Israel saying we are wrong, misguided and a cult, can be answered out of a book they believe in.

Baruch was Jeremiah the prophet’s scribe. Most of the prophets had scribes or recorders: Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Joshua. Baruch is one of them, and Baruch is basically Jeremiah’s words that Baruch wrote down.

“This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life.” Those that keep the commandments of this book come to life, and that comes from the words of Moses back in Deuteronomy 30 and many other places in Deuteronomy. “But such as leave it shall die”: back to blessing and cursing, life and death.

The law that endureth for ever. If Christ died and the law was done away with, what makes it a book of life any more? It would be no longer a book of life, just death, just a book. Like that pastor who sat down with the captain and said the Bible is flawed. He said what all the pastors believe, and that is why most of their Bibles stay closed: they just talk, or pull one verse and talk for four and five hours while money is collected and lives are destroyed and subverted.

“Turn thee, O Jacob, and take hold of it.” Turn thee who? O Jacob. Not all nations, not everybody, not the rainbow coalition. O Jacob. Take hold of the commandment of life, the book of life.

“Walk in the presence of the light thereof”: apply what is in it, “that thou mayest be illuminated.” A lot of black folks are afraid of the Illuminati, the Masons, skull and crossbones and the secret families. The Bible says keeping his laws you become truly illuminated, truly enlightened. Not Satan’s enlightenment; that’s garbage, that’s temporary. God’s laws are light: the same laws a lot of Christian churches refuse to apply and teach, saying they are done away with.

“Give not thine honour to another, nor the things that are profitable unto thee to a strange nation.” Do not give the nations the understanding God gave you; going back to verse 1, don’t give it to them. Israel tended to take what God gave us, the commandments of God, the Bible, and teach strange nations.

God did want Israel to teach the nations, but while we were ruling. Once Israel shared its understanding with the nations while we were captive, they learned from us and then took what we taught them and turned against us.

During the Holy Roman Empire there were black Caesars, basically white guys in black skin: Constantine and his mother, Emperor Justinian, Caracalla, evil as hell. After the late 100s A.D. the understanding of the Bible was lost, and anyone who taught the laws of Moses was killed, because the laws of Moses are still the words of Christ and were in complete opposition to the Roman social life. So many Israelites fled into Europe, between the Black and Caspian Seas, into the area called Khazaria, now known as the Ukraine, and lived there as refugees. The people in that land were called Khazars, which goes back to the word Caesars, pushed over there when black folks took Rome. That land was neutral, with paganism in it, and Israel taught them our laws. They learned the laws of our God, became converts, said now we have power, and those same converts ended up gaining our land in 1948.

Another way: Israel lived in the Sudan and the Sahara. Muhammad, a camel driver, illiterate, came across the Jews in the desert, and we taught him and even helped further his religion. Once he gained enough people to believe the doctrine he learned from us, he persecuted us, killed us by the thousands and enslaved us. There is even a history of an Israelite woman trying to poison him because he killed her family.

So whenever Israel gives our laws to the nations while captive, they take it, overthrow us, adopt our doctrine and say they are us. Now the Muslims say they are the chosen people rather than Israel, and the so-called Israelis say they are Jews rather than us.

“O Israel, happy are we: for things that are pleasing to God are made known unto us.” That is an exclusive statement. Christianity, and the Catholic Church it derives from, has made the Bible catholic, universal. It is originally and still a personal book, given to a particular people by a particular people for a particular people: the personal record of a nation of people.

“Be of good cheer, my people, the memorial of Israel. Ye were sold to the nations”: keep that in mind, sold to the nations. Baruch is a very small book, but there is a lot in it.

“Not for your destruction”, not to destroy you entirely, “but because ye moved God to wrath”: because we pissed God off. “Ye were delivered unto the enemies”, enemies plural.

“For I saw the captivity of my sons and daughters, which the Everlasting brought upon them.” This is Jerusalem speaking, our mother, our land, speaking to us: the Most High speaking to us through the spirit in terms of Jerusalem.

“With joy did I nourish them; but sent them away with weeping and mourning. Let no man rejoice over me, a widow.” The widow is Jerusalem our mother, “forsaken of many, who for the sins of my children am left desolate”: for the sins of my children I, Jerusalem, am left desolate.

“Because they departed from the law of God.” Their land was laid desolate based upon them departing from the law of God.

“They knew not his statutes, nor walked in the ways of his commandments, nor trod in the paths of discipline in his righteousness.” The path of discipline is righteousness, which is the laws and commandments of God.

So far: in 4:1 they shall come to life; in verse 4 the things pleasing to God; in verse 6 delivered to the enemies; in verse 12 the law of God; in 13 discipline, which is righteousness.

“Let them that dwell about Sion come, and remember ye the captivity of my sons and daughters.” “For he hath brought a nation upon them from far, a shameless nation, and of a strange language, who neither reverenced old man, nor pitied child.” That is speaking of Babylon, but it goes even to later on: into Spain, Portugal, the Europeans.

“These have carried away the dear beloved children of the widow”: the dear beloved children. Keep that in mind. “And left her that was alone desolate without daughters.”

“But what can I help you?” How can I help you, says God. “For he that brought these plagues upon you will deliver you from the hands of your enemies.” He that brought the plagues upon you will be the one to deliver you from the hands of your enemies.
“O Israel, how great is the house of God! and how large is the place of his possession!” We are the house of God; we are his possession.

“Great, and hath none end; high, and unmeasurable.” The house of God, Israel, is great and has no end. That sounds familiar. The class starts with the old first, because the same terminologies are used in the new: when the disciples were teaching the gospel there were no letters, no Matthew, Mark, Luke or John written yet.

precepts.why:
“But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.” Israel is the house that is great and has none end: Israel is a world without end.

And that is the world that God so loved. The old already said it before the new used the same words.

sense.text:
Baruch is a very heavy book: few chapters, but a lot in it, and it is basically Jeremiah’s words that Baruch wrote down.

“Put off, O Jerusalem, the garment of mourning and affliction, and put on the comeliness of the glory that cometh from God for ever”: put off, O Jews, the garment of mourning and affliction. “Cast about thee a double garment of the righteousness which cometh from God; and set a diadem on thine head of the glory of the Everlasting.”

“For God will shew thy brightness unto every country under heaven.” God is going to put Israel on top of the planet as a ruling nation of people on the earth, and then we will teach the nations. That is the time to do it, when we are ruling; not while we are captive, refugees, scattered and dispersed. That is what Baruch said in 4:3: don’t do that.

When Baruch wrote this, Babylon had overthrown us, and Jeremiah was travelling to our brothers and sisters who were refugees in Egypt, upper and lower Egypt, hiding from and running from the Babylonians. When you are captive and brought low, it is not the time to teach these nations. Our goal is to rule, and once we are ruling, then we teach the nations.
“For thy name shall be called of God for ever The peace of righteousness, and The glory of God’s worship.”

“Arise, O Jerusalem”: that is the context. “And stand on high”: where is that? Back in verse 3, unto every country under heaven. We are going to stand on high.

“And look about toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west unto the east”: from this side, back to our homeland again, from the west to the east, “by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of God.”

“For they departed from thee on foot, and were led away of their enemies: but God bringeth them unto thee exalted with glory, as children of the kingdom.” Keep in mind the children gathered from the west unto the east; it comes up again. The children of the kingdom gathered and exalted with glory are God’s sons and daughters. That is not all nations; all nations are not gathered from the west to the east.

“For God hath appointed that every high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and valleys filled up, to make even the ground, that Israel may go safely in the glory of God.”

Every high hill means the governing powers, the nations. The banks of long continuance are the rivers, the streams: that is the nations. They will be cast down, and Daniel 7:9 shows the same thing: the thrones cast down.

“I beheld till the thrones were cast down.” The thrones are the nations: it goes back to every high hill and the banks of long continuance in Baruch 5:7. These are thrones, kingdoms, and they are cast down.

“And the Ancient of days did sit.” The Ancient of days is the heavenly Father, sitting down on his behind, because he has a body to sit on. “Whose garment was white as snow”: he had clothing on, and to have clothing on you must have a body to wear it on.

“And the hair of his head like the pure wool”: woolly hair, black man hair, negro hair.

“His throne was like the fiery flame.” What does a puff of smoke need a throne for? A throne is a seat, and you sit with a body. A spirit can’t sit; it’s a puff of smoke, apparently, for these Christians. Y’all crazy.

Pastor Gino said in one of his videos that God made Adam a black man, and his woman too, and all men come from a black couple; that is why he calls the white man his brother. He is our brother, but he is evil and wicked as hell and will be judged for it despite his relation to us, because he broke that covenant. And God made Adam in his image. If God made Adam in his image, God has to have an image; otherwise Adam was made from nothing, because God is a puff of smoke?

precepts.why:
Here is how his Son looks. “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things”: the Son inherits what God established. “By whom also he made the worlds”: God used his Son to make the worlds, more than one world.

“Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.” To have a person means to have a persona, a body: a head, arms, legs, feet. Not the express image of a smoke. Express has the meaning exactly resembling the original, as the impress of a seal resembles the figure engraved on it: you take the seal and press it into the wax, and it leaves the exact same imprint as the seal. The Greek is literally an engraving, an impression, and express image is a good translation: there is no flaw in this translation, it means exactly what it says.

So Christ is the impression of his Father: the Father impressed and printed his own face on his Son’s face. When Christ walked this earth he was the exact resemblance of the original God; he looked just like his Father. When they asked him to show them the Father, Christ said you see him right here, I look just like him. Adam looked like the Father too, because he was made in his image. How hard is this? Why are they confused? Maybe you hate yourself. And what do they say: the filthy dirty black skin that God gave Christ? Shame on you.

So when you see the Son, you see the express image of what we read in Daniel 7:9: the hair of his head like the pure wool.

Some say Christ walked around as a white man and then changed when he was in his glory, or that he looked black but had a white head and white hairs. No: Daniel 7:9 says the hair of his head like the pure wool, and Christ is the express image of that. Christ is not going to walk around with a white head and white beard. He was not a mutant, not an X-Man; that’s not biblical.

“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.” The same way he left, in that same body, he will come back: angelic, full of God’s power, his original power. So there is no denying it: when Christ walked this earth he looked just like his Father, he left looking like his Father, and he will return looking like his Father.

sense.text: Back to Baruch 5: “For God hath appointed that every high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and valleys filled up, to make even the ground, that Israel may go safely in the glory of God”. These high hills and banks are the thrones of the nations that Daniel saw cast down.

“Moreover even the woods and every sweetsmelling tree shall overshadow Israel by the commandment of God. For God shall lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy and righteousness that cometh from him.” With mercy and righteousness that comes from him, God will lead Israel into glory.

You do not see Gentiles anywhere in these verses. Hold on to that mercy and righteousness; Zacharias speaks of the same tender mercy of our God in Luke 1.

Earlier in Baruch 4:13 it said the paths of discipline are his commandments. Now: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit”. The holy spirit of what? Discipline. Another word for spirit is ghost; holy ghost and holy spirit are synonymous. So the Holy Ghost is the ghost of discipline, and it will “remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in.”

That is why Christ had twelve disciples: they were under the discipline of the commandments. The Holy Spirit is the spirit of discipline.

“For wisdom is a loving spirit”. Wisdom, God’s commandments, is a loving spirit; the Holy Spirit is wisdom. A lot of you Christian pastors, modern Christianity cult leaders, do not have the Holy Ghost. The spirit is not in you. You’re running around having seizures, looking crazy; you got some kind of disease going on. That’s not the Holy Spirit. You’re making that up. It’s an act, a show, a performance.

“And will not acquit a blasphemer of his words”. Blasphemy is a man that says he has done greater works than Christ. No you haven’t … no you have not. No one has, because the Father through his Son made the worlds. Have you made worlds before? Have you made angels, made planets? The hell you talking about? This is your leader, this is your pastor. “For God is witness of his reins, and a true beholder of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue.”

Let’s not leave that thought about the Holy Spirit or Holy Ghost being one and the same. This history goes into John the Baptist’s parents. John the Baptist was in the truth when he was in the womb, in the truth out of the womb, and in the truth when he died. Anyone saying something different is a stupid ass; that is blasphemous in itself, to say he wasn’t.

“A certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia: and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth.”

“And they were both righteous before God”: John the Baptist’s parents were both righteous before God, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.”

So being righteous means you are walking in the commandments, blameless. That is what righteousness means in the New Testament: walking in all the commandments. How you get around that, Christians, Christian cult members?

They were righteous, keeping the commandments, him and his wife. “And his father Zacharias was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied”. He was filled with the Holy Ghost, the Holy Spirit, because he was keeping the commandments, so the spirit spoke through him: a righteous man with discipline. Of the two of them, one prophesied to Mary and one prophesied regarding his son and regarding this nation.

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”. Keep that in mind. The word redeem is a big word, but very important to remember and understand. His people: is that everybody? No. God’s people is Israel.

Remember, there was no Luke when Zacharias was saying this, so where did he get it from? From the Old Testament. Some, like the Adventists, say yes, it pertained to the Israelites, but you could be a spiritual Israelite, a child of God. That is not what the Bible is talking about.

“And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David”. You know it is referring to Israel literally, because the house of his servant David was the king over all twelve tribes. Not spiritual people: the children of a nation, Israel.

“As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us”. When he says we, he’s referring to himself and his wife. He is Israel, he is a Levite; both of them are the children of Aaron. So he is saying we should be saved from our enemies: the same thing Baruch said earlier in Baruch 4:21, deliver them out of the hand of their enemies.

“To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; The oath which he sware to our father Abraham”. These are possessive words: us, we, our fathers. It’s not spiritual Israel. Our fathers is a race, a bloodline: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob.

“That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear”: that’s Baruch 4:21 again. We might be able to serve him without being fearful for our lives, because serving God, keeping his commandments, cost us our lives. “In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life.”

“And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest”: your child John shall be called the prophet of the Highest. So how is it a man that was out of the truth? That’s some stupid stuff, some … doctrine. The prophet of the Highest; no one greater. “For thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways”.

“To give knowledge of salvation unto his people”: knowledge of how to be saved, to his people, “by the remission of their sins”. Their sins: not everyone, not all nations.

Once you have reading comprehension, that is very easy to be understood; you don’t have to go to college or have a bachelor’s. His people. But the Christians are going to read that and still reject it, even if it’s the New Testament, because our people is a stiff-necked and rebellious people, and these pastors don’t really want to serve God and don’t really believe what this Bible says. That’s why they’re going to reject what we just read.

“Through the tender mercy of our God”: remember earlier, Baruch 5:9 said he will lead his people Israel with mercy and righteousness. “Whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us”. The dayspring is Christ: he is the dayspring from on high, the light from on high, that visited us.

“To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death”: Christ came to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, “to guide our feet into the way of peace.” The way of peace is out of the shadow of death, out of darkness. That’s Israel he’s referring to.

precepts.why: His people: is that everybody? “And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.” My people Israel. So God’s people is Israel.

Get the Old Testament, because there was no Luke when Zacharias was saying this; who are his people? “But Pharaoh shall not hearken unto you, that I may lay my hand upon Egypt, and bring forth mine armies, and my people the children of Israel”.

So God’s people in the Old Testament is the children of Israel, and God’s people in the New Testament is the children of Israel. When you read my people anywhere in the Bible, it is God’s people the children of Israel, hands down. You can’t be a Jew inwardly; you have to be a Jew outwardly.

sense.text:
Going back to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death: David prophesied of this, and this is where Zacharias is quoting from. He is not quoting from Luke. When Zacharias said this there was no Matthew, no Mark, no Corinthians, no Colossians, no Jude, no Revelation, no first, second or third John. These were not written yet. The gospels came later; they weren’t quoting from the letters of Paul or out of the New Testament, quote unquote.

“Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron”. Affliction and iron is slavery: yokes of iron upon your neck, your hands, your ankles. It’s slavery that it’s talking about.

“Because they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High”. Because they rebelled against the words of God they were taken into captivity, or slavery; being in captivity and slavery are synonymous.

“Therefore he brought down their heart with labour”: labour is slavery, captivity. “They fell down, and there was none to help”: there was no one to save them, no one to redeem them. Here David is quoting Moses.

“Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble, and he saved them out of their distresses.” Israel was in captivity over and over again, because the curses of Moses were reoccurring. They weren’t one time, all at once; they happened multiple times through the course of time, because Moses said it was going to happen to you and your children. These are generational curses, not once in a lifetime like you Christians try to push. Y’all as stupid as hell; stop challenging us.

“He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death”. The darkness is captivity, and the shadow of death is captivity too. Why? Because Israel being captive under the nations is like death. We’re not ruling; the nations overthrow us, push their doctrines on us and remove us from our laws, and we become spiritually dead. That’s why it’s called the shadow of death: we’re not quite dead, but we are spiritually dead when we go among the nations and they enforce their doctrines upon us. We begin to assimilate. That’s the shadow of death.

“And brake their bands in sunder.” He would always save us, but eventually he stopped doing that: you guys are rebellious, I’m going to keep you there for a while now. And we are still there today, until we are sealed.

precepts.why:
David is quoting Moses, not Luke and Mark. “And the Lord shall bring thee into Egypt again with ships, by the way whereof I spake unto thee, Thou shalt see it no more again”. You will not see little Egypt again as a nation; that never happened again the same way. Israel got an exodus out of Egypt as a nation one time. This would be a different Egypt, a different form of slavery, by way of ships, because you walked there the first time. This Egypt you are going to be brought to by ships.

“And there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen”: labour. “And no man shall buy you”: no man shall redeem you. That is the same thing as Psalms 107:12, “he brought down their heart with labour; they fell down, and there was none to help.” The same exact words.

sense.text: “I the Lord have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles”. He’s talking about Christ here. Some see right there, a light of the Gentiles, and say the other nations. But there’s a comma: the thought continues.

“To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.” So the Gentiles sit in darkness. Who is sitting in darkness? Darkness is captivity. So the Gentiles in this verse are the Israelites in captivity. The prison house is the land of your captivity: we are prisoners in these lands of captivity.
“I am the Lord: that is my name: and my glory”.

precepts.why:
“And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not”: earlier, in verse 7, it was to open the blind eyes and bring out the prisoners from the prison. So he is elaborating on who he was referring to back in verse 6, the people, the light of the Gentiles. “I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight”: the evil, crooked things around them made straight, the straight path.

“These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.” That’s the people of Israel, and the Gentiles there is Israel. “They shall be turned back, they shall be greatly ashamed, that trust in graven images, that say to the molten images, Ye are our gods”: a people scattered abroad serving other gods.

“The Lord is well pleased for his righteousness’ sake; he will magnify the law, and make it honourable”, as Christ came to do. Christ came to magnify the law: he pulled the law out and made it of more importance. Magnify means to enhance it.

“But this is a people robbed and spoiled”: this is the people he is going to bring light to. Robbed and spoiled goes back to them being blind, to them being in darkness. “They are all of them snared in holes, and they are hid in prison houses”: who? The people of Israel, the Gentiles. It’s the same people. Israel is called Gentiles in the Old Testament: that’s the northern kingdom, and he was referring to both houses, Judah and Israel. Y’all don’t know the Bible. When you read Paul saying Gentiles in the New Testament you say, oh yeah, anybody; but the prophets used the same terminology, calling the Israelites Gentiles. “They are for a prey, and none delivereth; for a spoil, and none saith, Restore.”

“Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers?” There you go. Who’s Jacob? All twelve tribes. That’s who is in the prison houses, that’s who the light is set for, that’s who is in darkness, that’s who is blind. “Did not the Lord, he against whom we have sinned? for they would not walk in his ways, neither were they obedient unto his law.”

So the people of Israel in verse 6, and the Gentiles, is all twelve tribes. That’s who he is talking about.

sense.text:
“Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali”: that’s the northern kingdom. “And afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.” Naphtali, Zebulun, Galilee: those are the lands in the northern kingdom. This is Samaria here.

What’s the dimness? Dimness is when you can’t see; it’s dark. You dim the lights, you make it darker in the room. Dimness and darkness are the same thing.

“The people that walked in darkness”: the people of Naphtali, Zebulun, those in Galilee. “Have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death”: that’s the Israelites. “Upon them hath the light shined”, because Christ would come and teach them later on.

Isaiah is prophesying of Christ’s coming, here in chapter 9 and in chapter 42: coming to visit the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. That’s what he came to do while they were in the valley of the shadow of death, in darkness, in their lands being colonized by nations at the time, whether the Assyrians who put nations in their land, or the Babylonians, the Persians, the Greeks, the Romans residing there. He would visit them in the lands in which they were colonized.

That’s why the Samaritan woman at the well said we know that Messiah cometh: she understood what we are reading here in Isaiah. That Samaritan woman was an Israelite. Samaria was the capital of Ephraim; she was of the northern kingdom of Israel that was in darkness. Christ is that light, and through him coming and dying they were able to repent.
“Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee”. At this point John the Baptist, his cousin, is in prison, and Christ goes to Galilee.

“And leaving Nazareth”: he left his home town, “and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim”. That is the same place as Isaiah 9:1, the land of the northern kingdom.

“That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet”. By Christ visiting that area he fulfilled what Isaiah spoke: “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles”. Christ is fulfilling Isaiah 9:1 and 2.

The people there are Israelites, the northern kingdom, and Matthew calls it Galilee of the Gentiles. These are Gentiles living among Gentiles: Israelites in darkness, in their lands colonized by the nations. Whether it be the Assyrians who put nations in their land, the Babylonians, the Persians, the Greeks or the Romans residing there, Christ would visit them in the lands they were colonized in and scattered amongst.

“The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.” That region is called darkness and the shadow of death because it was colonized. In the time of the Assyrians nations were placed there, they never left, and Ephraim was assimilated amongst them. How is light sprung up? Because Christ showed up. He is that light, the dayspring that Zechariah mentioned, visiting and redeeming his people. Through him coming and dying they were able to repent.

That is why the Samaritan woman at the well said she knew Messiah cometh. She understood what is read in Isaiah, because she was an Israelite: Samaria was the capital of Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel that was in darkness. And Christ told her, ‘you worship but you know not what you worship’, and ‘salvation is of Judah’: you got to be taught by Judah, which is in Christ.

“From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” From this time his ministry began. Matthew 1 and Luke 1 go together, Matthew 2 and Luke 2, Matthew 3 and Luke 3, Matthew 4 and Luke 4 are tied together: this is the beginning of his ministry, and later in Matthew 4 he calls the disciples, ‘follow me, we got work to do.’

“Have ye understood all these things?” He was reminding them of the kingdom to come, and the disciples answered “Yea, Lord”: they got it.

You Christians don’t even go in the Old Testament, because you don’t understand it. You were not institutionalized in the Old Testament; your master taught you the New and Psalms.

“Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven”: every scribe or prophet, like Baruch was. If you are instructed in the doctrine of Christ, in how to get to the kingdom of heaven, you are “like unto a man that is an householder”. A householder takes care of the house, and the house here is the house of Israel. We’re the householders. You Christians are slumlords, you ain’t no householders, you drug dealers, hirelings.

“Which bringeth forth out of his treasure”: his treasure is his Bible, and what he brings out of it is his actions, his words, his works, his deeds. And he brings forth “things new and old”. When you’re a scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven you bring out of the new and the old, both testaments. You pastors are finished: all you do is bring out the new.

You cannot bring out the new without the old; there would be no new without the old. In Matthew 4 Christ referenced Isaiah 9:1. The gospels have no meaning without the Old Testament, because they were preaching from the old. The gospels are a confirmation of what is prophesied to come by the law and the prophets; they recorded what Christ did based upon prophecies you must read in the old. To understand the gospels you must read the Old Testament. New and old, you need both, and that includes the sayings of the seers, which today is wrongfully called the Apocrypha: same people, same thing, Old Testament.

“That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.” This goes in conjunction with Baruch 5:5, read earlier, where he gathers his people from the west unto the east; add it to your precepts.

A lot of times Christians read this and say, see, that’s talking about the Gentiles. No, that’s not talking about Gentiles. The many that shall come from the east and the west are the twelve tribes that are scattered. Add that precept to your artillery.

“But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will be back too, but the wicked elders are not going to make it. The children of the kingdom here are the Pharisees, and you pastors, you elders, you Christian cult member leaders: that’s you, you’re the evil elders of the kingdom, you’re going to die here.

You are the Pharisees and Sadducees, and worse than them. The Pharisees at least taught the law and didn’t keep it; you teach there’s no law at all. Calling you a Pharisee is a compliment, because Christ said of the Pharisees, observe and do what they say, and we can’t even tell anybody to do what you say, because you don’t do nothing.

precepts.why:
Throw some salt in the wound: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will save my people from the east country, and from the west country; And I will bring them, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.”

It is his people, Israel, that he saves from the east and the west and brings to Jerusalem. This is Old Testament, and that’s where Christ is quoting from when he says many shall come from the east and west. Nowhere to go, nowhere to run, nowhere to hide; and there is a lot more, way more, than that. Write it down and use it.

sense.text: “Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.” At this point Christ is dead and resurrected; he rolled out the grave. The disciples went to the gravesite and found he wasn’t there, and now they’re going back confused because he’s gone. “But their eyes were holden that they should not know him”: Christ approached them, but their eyes were kept so they wouldn’t recognize it was him.

“What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad?” Christ is asking them what’s wrong with you, what you talking about, why are you so sad. Cleopas answers, “Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem”, and they tell him “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people”.

“And how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him.” It doesn’t say the whole nation of Israel. It says the rulers and the chief priests had him killed, them and their followers, not the entire nation of Jews. You Christians say the nation denied him; that’s not what the disciples are saying.

“But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel”. What did the disciples believe? That he was going to redeem Israel. Not everybody, not all nations, not LGBT. That is what Zechariah said in Luke 1:68, that he hath visited and redeemed his people, and his disciples believed the same thing. Does it say spiritual Israel? No. So it’s Israel.

To redeem is, first, to purchase back: to regain possession of by payment of a stipulated price, to repurchase. The re- is the again. To purchase back means you bought it before and now you’re buying it back again; to regain means you had it before and you’re gaining it again. If I sell my car and then go buy it back from them, that car was mine initially. Like going to a pawn shop: you sell an old watch, then go back and buy it again. Or if I owe a man money and can’t pay, I might give him my son or my daughter as a servant to pay off the debt, and I go redeem my child by paying him the money. That’s exactly the same thing.

It is also to ransom, liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage, or from any obligation or liability to suffer or to be forfeited, by paying a price or ransom. The liability is sin, and the price was his Son on the cross. And hence, to rescue and deliver from the bondage of sin and the penalties of God’s violated law. He came to redeem his people: to buy back what was once his before.

“To day is the third day since these things were done.”

Certain women of their company were early at the sepulchre, “And when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive.” He visited the women first, Mary first. And certain of them went to the sepulchre, “but him they saw not”: they didn’t find his body.

“O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken”. Remember, they don’t know who he is; he held their eyes. And he says, you guys are stupid, you guys are foolish. Slow of heart: your heart is your mind, and your mind is slow. Christ called his own friends, his own disciples, fools; he called them names. But when we do it, we’re evil and full of hate. That’s that cult mentality, that institutionalized church mindset.
“Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?”

“And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.” Slow that down. Beginning at Moses. Not Matthew, not John, not Luke, not Mark, not Jude, not Philemon, not Colossians, not Paul. Beginning at Moses, and all the prophets: Christ expounded unto them out of Moses and the prophets all things concerning himself, like we’re doing tonight.

precepts.why:
“Fear and dread shall fall upon them; by the greatness of thine arm”: upon the Egyptians. “They shall be as still as a stone; till thy people pass over, O Lord”: his people, Israel, pass over, “till the people pass over, which thou hast purchased.”

God purchased Israel. He killed the nations in exchange for their debts, as a ransom; he got us. This is the first purchase, the one that redemption buys back again.

“O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?” Then: “Remember thy congregation”. The congregation is your church, a church assembly of people. “Which thou hast purchased of old”: where did they get that from? Exodus 15:16. “The rod of thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed”, because David is prophesying of his son dying on the cross and redeeming us, buying us again. “This mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.”

So when God redeems his people, he buys back what he purchased of old. That’s not all nations: all nations cannot be redeemed, because they were never purchased to begin with.

The church he redeemed is the church of old that he purchased, and when Christ died on the cross he bought them again. Israel was indebted to the old covenant, which is sacrifice. Christ died on the cross as a ransom to get us out of that debt of the sacrificial law, granting us a new chance at life in the New Testament. That’s all it means. We are still obligated to keep the commandments, but not to sacrifice.

sense.text:
“This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you”. Now we go to the New Testament. These words are not being used for no reason: who is beloved? You’re not going to find my beloved Canaanites, my beloved Moabites, my beloved …, my beloved Ammonites; that ain’t in the Bible. One nation is beloved, not everybody. The beloved are the Israelites.

Now we know who Peter was talking to. “In both which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance”: remember what?

“That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour”. They were taught and instructed by the words of the holy prophets as well as by the epistles of the apostles, and the apostles were preaching from the Old Testament.

precepts.why: Going back to Baruch 4:16, his beloved children: “These have carried away the dear beloved children of the widow, and left her that was alone desolate without daughters.” His dear beloved children is referring to Israel. So when Peter writes to the beloved, he is writing to Israel.

“Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”, “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God”. Who was elect according to the foreknowledge of God, God’s knowledge before? Who did God acknowledge before?

Beloved and elect are Old Testament words. Peter was not quoting from his own letters; that doesn’t make no damn sense. He’s quoting from the law and the prophets.

“For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect”. Israel is his elect. That’s why Peter is saying these words, beloved and elect, to the strangers scattered abroad: they are Old Testament words for Israel.

He is still talking to the strangers of chapter 1 verse 1, the strangers in Pontus, Bithynia and Asia who are called the elect. Now what does he say about them? “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”. Who is referred to as an holy nation and a peculiar people? Everybody? Show me holy …, holy Canaanites, holy Hivites, holy Midianites. Show me one precept in the Old Testament where other nations are called holy outside of his own people.

“That ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness”: darkness and the shadow of death, the same thing as Isaiah 9:1 and 2, “into his marvellous light”.

“Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” He’s quoting Hosea. That’s not talking about strangers as in other nations or Gentiles. He’s talking to the children of Israel, who were referred to as strangers because they were scattered in strange lands.

sense.text: “Wherefore, beloved”: the beloved are the peculiar people, the holy nation Peter called them in 1 Peter 2:9, the Israelites. “Be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.” How? By keeping the commandments.

“Even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you”: Paul wrote to these same people. That was Paul’s office, to teach the scattered Israelites abroad.

Why did Paul write to them? Because Paul was the apostle to the Gentiles, the strangers scattered abroad, and those are the very people Peter is writing to: the ones he called the elect according to the foreknowledge of God, the holy, peculiar people of 1 Peter 2:9. Those are the Gentiles Paul was writing to. Peter is confirming right here who Paul is writing to in all his letters, and that right there is enough.

“As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood”: things in Paul’s letters that are hard to understand, “which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures”. The other scriptures are the Old Testament. Paul wrote his letters based upon the other scriptures, so if you are unlearned and unstable and you are wrestling with the Old Testament, you will not understand Paul’s letters. That is what Peter is telling you.

“Unto their own destruction.” You Christians are guilty of this right here, and your Christian cult leaders are guilty of this scripture right here, because you are unstable and unlearned and wrestle the other scriptures. The leaders know their congregants don’t read for themselves, so they pull complicated chapters out of Paul’s letters to confound their followers, because they themselves are confounded and unlearned in what they are reading. And all of a sudden Paul’s an apostate, Paul is not a prophet, the Bible’s flawed, you’ve done greater works than Christ, you’re gonna eat pork, you’re gonna eat shrimp, you don’t gotta grow your beard, it’s not literal, it’s spiritual, it’s metaphoric. You just get worse and worse.

It is not what happened to Paul himself that matters, he was killed, but what happened to his teaching. Even while Paul lived, the people he preached to misunderstood him, and Peter gave the warning: Paul’s letters are hard to understand if you do not read the Old Testament. Paul urged men to have faith in Christ’s death and in Christ being the Messiah, and to lead a godly life themselves, and personal righteousness is keeping the commandments. That is how you become godly or righteous, like John the Baptist’s parents, who kept the commandments; people like that would survive God’s judgment.

But most who listened to Paul remembered only believing in Christ and grace and mercy, the resurrection and eternal life. That is Christians today: you believe in Christ dying and in grace, and you deliberately skip the middle step, living godly lives by keeping the commandments. Faith in Christ alone became the entire basis of the religion of the pagan Christians, and that is Christianity today.

The Judeo-Christians uphold the law with faith in Christ; those two go together, they are one and the same. That is what we do. The disciples were Judeo-Christians, early Christians, Jewish Christians, the same people: they kept the law while firmly believing in Christ. In the book of Acts the Israelites following Christ in keeping the commandments were called Christians at Antioch; those are the real Christians, not these pagan Christians today.

But the pagan Christian attitude won in the end. It is the largest church system on the planet, with Islam in second place, and it won because no laws were involved: the churches are full because there is no accountability, the middle step is done away with. That paganism everybody follows today is the other Jesus and the other gospel Paul warned of, and Christ warned that many shall come in his name and deceive many. And when we bring the truth, they call us racist, legalists, evil, because we say Christ came and died only for Israel, and that’s what the Bible says. We keep warning you about pastors like Gino Jennings, but a lot of you are not listening.

Pagans who admired the Bible and how its stories sound can now follow a god that lets them do what they want: God knows your heart, we all fall short, keep the sabbath any day you want, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, celebrate Easter and Christmas. Most converts became pagan Christians because of those laws, that middle step. Our people didn’t want it in Moses’ time, in the prophets’ time, or in Christ’s time, and they don’t want it now. Christ and the disciples and apostles warned us of it, and many of you watching right now, angry, are victims of this doctrine: a religion that appeals to you because you enjoy how the Bible sounds, like a lovely song, as Ezekiel said, without doing what it says.

This is a conversation between two Jews, two Israelites: one a ruler of the Jews, Nicodemus, and the other the King of the Jews, Christ. It is about being born again, salvation, and accepting Christ as Saviour. Christ is not quoting John; John recorded the conversation between two Israelite men. It is not a conversation about everybody, all nations; two of the same people talking about all nations doesn’t make any sense.

“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up”: even so means the same way. The same way Moses lifted the serpent up in the wilderness, the Son of man must be lifted up as well, for the same reason. Hold on to that, because Christ is pulling this from the law, from Numbers 21.

precepts.why:
“And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water”. “And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.” Among who? The people of Israel. Israel was complaining, and these are the victims, the people of Israel.

“Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord, and against thee; pray unto the Lord, that he take away the serpents from us. And Moses prayed for the people.” The Lord told Moses, “Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.” Moses made “a serpent of brass” and lifted it up on the pole, and “when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.”

That is the serpent Christ means in John 3:14: the Son of man lifted up the same way, for the same people, Israel.

Wisdom explains what that serpent in Numbers represented. “For when the horrible fierceness of beasts came upon these, and they perished with the stings of crooked serpents”: that is Numbers 21. “Thy wrath endured not for ever”: he didn’t kill Israel off; it was a temporary punishment. “But they were troubled for a small season”: Israel was troubled for a small season, “that they might be admonished”, warned.

“Having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law.” The serpent was a sign of salvation, and it was symbolic of Christ being lifted up. So Christ is a sign of salvation for us, to put us in remembrance to keep the commandments of God. That is what he is for. That is why the ambulance has the serpent on its emblem: it heals people, it saves people. That is the ambulance’s purpose, and Christ’s the same way.

“For he that turned himself toward it was not saved by the thing that he saw”: the one who turned toward that serpent lifted up was not saved by the serpent of brass itself; it was just brass. He was saved “by thee, that art the Saviour of all”, by God himself.

“But thy sons”: thy sons, not all nations, not the mixed multitude. “Not the very teeth of venomous dragons overcame: for thy mercy was ever by them, and healed them.” God’s mercy healed them, not the serpent itself.

“For they were pricked, that they should remember thy words”: they were bitten so they would remember the law, remember they had sinned against God and against Moses, which is why they got bitten in the first place. They had to repent of their sins and not do it anymore, like Christ told the woman taken in adultery, sin no more. “And were quickly saved, that not falling into deep forgetfulness, they might be continually mindful of thy goodness.”

“For it was neither herb, nor mollifying plaister, that restored them to health: but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things.” No ointment healed those snake bites; the word did, the law. And that is Christ: he is the word also.

So Christ is a sign of salvation for us, to acknowledge his death and to put us in the mindset of keeping the laws. That is what his death was all about: to remember to keep his laws and commandments, with faith in his death.

sense.text: “And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.” Christ taught his disciples out of the law of Moses and the prophets.

“All things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.” Written where? In the law of Moses, in the prophets and in the psalms. Christ preached from the Old Testament, the things concerning him. He was not preaching from his disciples’ gospels or Paul’s letters, and he was not coming off the top of his head, making it up, the way you Christians think. That is where he pulled John 3:14 from: Moses and the serpent in Numbers 21.

“That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” You will say verse 14 is Israel, but verse 15 is everybody, because it says whosoever. Remember this is a conversation between two men who were well versed in the laws. So when Christ told Nicodemus that whosoever believeth in him should not perish but have eternal life, the kingdom, he was getting that whosoever from the prophets, from Joel 2:32.

Christians read that whosoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved and get confused about what it means to be saved. They think you dip your head in water and when you die you go live up in the sky; that’s Greek mythology. Being saved is, first, being saved from your enemies, which is what Christ came to save us from. The second form of being saved is from the destruction coming on the earth in World War III. Those are the two forms of salvation the Bible speaks of: saved from your enemies, and saved in that time of trouble.

precepts.why:
“And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered”: delivered is saved, the same thing being said a different way. Whosoever where? “For in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance”: in mount Zion and in Jerusalem. Not in the United States, not in China: in Jerusalem shall be salvation, eternal life.

“As the lord hath said”: Joel is quoting the Lord, “and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.” The remnant whom the Lord shall call is the whosoever he is referring to. When did the Lord say this? Isaiah 10.

This is where the Lord said it, and Joel was confirming it about whosoever in mount Zion and Jerusalem. “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob”: the house of Jacob is all twelve tribes. They “shall no more again stay upon him that smote them”: they shall no longer be in captivity, “but shall stay upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.”

“The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God.” The remnant of the house of Jacob shall return and be saved, because all Israel ain’t gonna make it; a lot of them are gonna die. “For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness.” The consumption is the destruction: “For the Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land”, this land here.

So once again, the remnant whom the Lord shall call in Joel 2:32 is the remnant of the house of Jacob; Joel was quoting Isaiah 10. Whosoever in mount Zion and in Jerusalem, whom the Lord shall call, is the remnant of the house of Jacob. There is no way around this.

“And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people”. Who is Michael standing up for? The children of Daniel’s people, the Israelites. Not spiritual Israelites: the literal Israelites on the earth. That’s not hard to understand when you read about Michael, that angel, standing up in Revelation 12.

“And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time”: this is World War III. Are your pastors telling you there is a world war coming on this earth? Destruction is coming on this earth, and in the midst of that destruction is where Christ is going to return.

“And at that time thy people shall be delivered”: Daniel’s people. Delivered is the same thing as being saved: delivered from that destruction. That is the right understanding of what it means to be saved.

sense.text:
“For God so loved the world”: for means because, so verse 16 is continuing from verses 15 and 14. They are going to be saved like Israel was in the wilderness from the snake bites, because God so loved the world.

You Christians tend to run past these verses. Loved is past tense: I loved that movie, I loved that car, these are things I loved in the past; that is why it has the ed at the end. So what world did God love in the past? Show me the New Testament where God loved all nations. The world he so loved is Israel.

precepts.why:
“For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God: the Lord thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.” God makes it clear that being an Israelite is of extreme importance.

To say that doesn’t matter, to tell our people they have dirty, black, filthy, sinful skin, that’s madness, and it is hypocrisy, Gino Jennings. Pagan Christianity is the reason our people despise their black skin, because behind pagan Christianity is a pagan Caucasian Jesus that you hypocritically smack all around your stage. You tell people Christ came from a region where people were of color, black, which is commendable, and then turn around and tell us our skin is dirty and black and sinful. In pagan Christianity our people are forced, subliminally, to accept a Caucasian Christ, and if that Caucasian Christ is the express image of his Father, then God is white too, and white folks are in the image of God. Regardless of what you meant by it, you are reinforcing that narrative. It was foolish.

Read it again: God chose Israel “to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.” The Bible says God chose the Israelites and they are above all people. That is very standard English. So what you Christians are telling me is the Most High is a recovering racist, because to say, I created all people on the earth but you Israelites are my chosen people, I am only dealing with you, and you are above all people, is very different from what is taught in Christianity. Brothers and sisters, ask yourselves: are we going to follow Christianity, or what the Bible says?

God is declaring his race, his nation, to be above the other nations. Throughout history there is always one nation above the others; there has never been a time when all nations were equal in power. Even today America is on top, and soon she is going to be on the bottom in nuclear fire, and we are going to be on top. It is what it is.

“The Lord did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people: But because the Lord loved you, and because he would keep the oath which he had sworn unto your fathers, hath the Lord brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondmen, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” The Lord loved you: redemption and love go hand in hand. God loved his people based upon the love he had for their forefathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: a bloodline.

We came here to explain who God loved in John 3:16. “But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.”

“Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.” I will kill people for you. He did it to the Egyptians: he killed their firstborn, and that was the ransom used to redeem his people out of Egypt. I will destroy America for you; I will kill billions for you with nuclear destruction. That is what he is doing it for: he is going to kill billions to save a few million. It is what it is.

“But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation”: Israel shall be saved. That is the same salvation as Daniel 12:1, Joel 2:32 and Isaiah 10:20-23.

“Ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.” Israel is a world without end. God made the worlds, as read earlier in Hebrews 1, so which world does God love? The world of Israel that came out of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. That is the world he so loved, the world he killed nations for, the world that shall be saved with an everlasting salvation.

sense.text:
This is the pagan Christians’ favorite scripture: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost”. They hold it up and say, see brother, you can’t get around that: go and teach all nations, all nations can pray to God.

But “all nations” here is not every race on the face of the earth. Israel is the world God so loved, the world that shall be saved with an everlasting salvation, and Israel was scattered among all nations. Go to the other places the Christians run to with “all nations” and “every”, and the scriptures themselves show who Christ sent his disciples to.

precepts.why:
The Christians go here next: “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands”. It is the same thing used in Matthew 28: go forth and teach all nations, then a multitude no man could number of all nations.

It looks like it settles it, but this verse is repeating another verse the Christians never read, Revelation 5:9, and that one shows who this multitude is.

Luke is repeating what Matthew said in Matthew 28:19: “repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.” Remission of whose sins? Remember Zechariah in Luke said remission of their sins: the sins of his people.

It is to be preached “among all nations”, among them, “beginning at Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is where the Jews were initially, but where else are they? Among all nations too. So it is the same thing: the gospel goes to Israel where Israel is, starting at Jerusalem and then to those scattered among all the nations.

Revelation 7:9 is repeating Revelation 5:9. They sung a new song: “Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain”. That is Christ, slain, “and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation”. Revelation 7:9 said “of all”; this says “out of every”, and that is a big difference. He redeemed us out of every nation, kindred, tongue and people. Then verse 10: “And hast made us unto our God kings and priests: and we shall reign on the earth.” Reign on the earth.

To redeem means to purchase again, to buy again what was previously purchased. So to redeem them means they were his once before. When were all nations purchased by God? Show it in the Old Testament; you can’t go nowhere else. Find the Lord purchasing Moab or Edom or Amalek or Ammon or any other nation outside of Israel. You won’t.

Who did God purchase before, and why is he buying them again? Because they were sold off into captivity. Christ dying on the cross gave them the chance to be redeemed, so that when Christ returns he can save them from that captivity. That is what redemption is for: that we should be saved from our enemies, as Zechariah said in Luke 1.

“Out of every nation” sounds familiar: “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.” Jews, out of every nation under heaven. That is what Revelation 5:9 is talking about: Israelites, redeemed out of every kindred, tongue, people and nation, because that is where they were scattered.

sense.text:
The Christians run here too: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” Every creature, brother, see, everybody; you’re misled, you have hate in your heart.

So when he said every creature, there are many creatures today: animals and all of that. Did he come to save the fish in the sea and the rocks? Did he come to save the water bottles, the cups, the phones, the goats, the icicles? Every creature does not mean every living thing on the earth, and “all the world” does not mean every nation. The scriptures define both: all the world is wherever the Jews were scattered, and his creature is his people.

precepts.why:
They accused Paul: “we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world”. Among the Jews where? Throughout the world. All the Jews throughout the world: the scattered ones the apostles were sent to. That is “all the world” in Mark 16:15.

And there are Jews there. There are light ones there, not the white ones, unless they have black ancestry somewhere, and then them too. We don’t teach that you get salvation based upon the hue or the color of your skin. You got a lot of dark burnt … that’s going to die, the same as the light ones. What we teach is that Christ is going to come and save his people who are scattered abroad, who vary in features and shapes and sizes and colors, based upon bloodline.

And the white man’s penis is not powerful enough to penetrate every vagina on the earth and make half … all over the world; that’s white supremacy. They are not that fertile; in fact they’re dying off, and they are trying to preserve their kind, because their women don’t want to be mothers, they want to be business women like the men. They’ve always been the minorities. They overthrew us and told us that they were the minorities and labeled us minorities, but we outnumber everyone on the planet, that’s what God says, and we still do even in captivity. There’s no such thing as half white.

The Most High does not go by how you look; he goes by the father. David’s grandmother was a Moabite, but was David a mix? No, he was Israel, because his father was Judah. If your father is a white man, like the previous mayor of New York, de Blasio, a white man, an Edomite, whose kids are dark with afros, wide noses and big lips and don’t look like him, are his kids descendants of Israel? No. It’s not about how you look or complexion; it is the seed of Israel, and the seed of Israel has been scattered throughout the four corners of the earth. The nation of Israel in general are people of color, but there are exceptions to the rule: remnants of us scattered abroad who are high yellow or pale. It’s not a color thing, it’s a nation thing. But concerning Christ it is a color thing, because the scripture told us exactly: Christ is a very dark-skinned brother.

Thus saith the Lord, “which giveth the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar; The Lord of hosts is his name: If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the Lord, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever.” The seed of Israel is Jacob’s sperm. That means there is no such thing as Israel disappearing in the nations through blood mingling; that’s not biblical. If the sun, moon and stars no longer exist, then the seed of Israel is no more. Do they still exist? Yes. So Jacob’s descendants still exist despite so-called intermingling, being descendants through their father’s line. In Deuteronomy 28 the curse is upon your children: the seed still exists based upon the curses, no matter how you look.

That football player who took the knee, Colin Kaepernick, is very high yellow and his mother is white, but his father is Israel, so he is the seed. Drake’s kids, whatever they look like, are the seed of Israel; whether they repent is up to the Lord. We don’t teach that you have to look a certain way for salvation. It is all about the seed of Israel, and our people have mixed themselves among the nations. That is why in Revelation 7:9, when John saw them, he says different nations and tongues and people: they did not look like how Israel looked back then, they looked different from mixing among the nations, but they all are Israel.

Why did he say go into all nations? “And the Lord shall scatter you among the nations”. Because the Lord scattered Israel among all nations, he will redeem them from among the nations, the same as Revelation 5:9. “And ye shall be left few in number among the heathen, whither the Lord shall lead you.” Among the heathen, twice: Israel left few, among the heathen nations, wherever the Lord led them. That is all the world the disciples were sent into.

Now regarding every creature: “Be not wroth with us but spare thy people, and have mercy upon thine own inheritance: for thou art merciful unto thy creature.” Spare thy people; have mercy upon thine own inheritance, the people he purchased of old, as in Exodus 15:16. “For thou art merciful unto thy creature”: his creature is his people, among every nation, in all nations, among the people on the earth. That’s his creature, and that is the every creature of Mark 16:15.

This is the lion, that’s Christ: “For the rest of my people shall he deliver with mercy”. The rest is the remnant, my people, the Hebrews. He shall deliver them, save them, with mercy, those upon his borders, “and he shall make them joyful until the coming of the day of judgment”. The ones Christ delivers are the rest of his people.

“The same is he whom God the Highest hath kept a great season”: Christ, his son, “which by his own self shall deliver his creature”. His creature is his people; you can’t get around this. “And he shall order them that are left behind”: those that are left are the remnants. It is repetitive with Isaiah 10:20-22, the remnant of Israel that shall return.

Same chapter, the ones left behind named: “But those that be left behind of thy people are they that are found within my borders.” Those left behind are of thy people. So the creature Christ shall deliver is God’s people, Israel, that’s among all nations.

“For the whole creature in his proper kind was fashioned again anew”. The whole creature is the whole nation. Fashioned again anew is born again, made again anew. How? “Serving the peculiar commandments that were given unto them”: serving the peculiar commandments is what made them a peculiar people, going back to 1 Peter 2:9 and 10. “That thy children might be kept without hurt”: thy children, kept without hurt by keeping the commandments.

So the whole creature is the Israelites. That is who the gospel was preached to when he said every creature.

sense.text:
Paul: “Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come”. Saying nothing else but what Moses and the prophets said.

Every single letter Paul wrote was based upon the words of Moses and the prophets. He wasn’t pulling from Matthew, he wasn’t pulling from Mark, Jude or John; he was pulling from the law and the prophets. Christ pulled from the law and the prophets, and Peter pulled from the law and the prophets. When you read Paul’s letters and think he is saying don’t keep the laws, you don’t know what you’re talking about. The law doesn’t say thou shalt not keep what the law says.

precepts.why:
At this point Paul is in Rome on house arrest, and the elders of the Jews of the synagogues in Rome came to visit him in his lodging, “to whom he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.” Paul taught Christ out of the law of Moses and the prophets, from morning hours to evening hours.

“And some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not.” The ones that believed and did not believe, Paul wrote to them: that is the letter to the Romans. Acts 28 is the introduction to the letter to the Romans, written to the Jews of Rome, not literal ethnic Italians, but the Israelites living in Rome and the synagogues they ran there. Our people are so simple they read the book of Romans and think it is talking about white people. It is not.

“Well spake the Holy Ghost by Esaias the prophet unto our fathers”. By who? Esaias. Paul is not quoting Matthew, he’s not quoting Jude; he is quoting Isaiah, because he taught out of the law and the prophets: “Hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and not perceive”.

“Be it known therefore unto you, that the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and that they will hear it.” We showed you from the Old Testament, in Isaiah 42, that the Gentiles are a part of Israel. They will hear it because Christ said his sheep hear his voice, and a stranger will not. The Gentiles hear because they are his sheep.

“And when he had said these words, the Jews departed”. Who departed? Not the Italians, not the Spaniards: the Jews. And while Paul was under house arrest he wrote to them, and that’s how Romans starts, just as Ruth comes after Judges and took place during the time of the Judges. You better know these things.

sense.text: “But unto them that are contentious, and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, indignation and wrath”: those who go against the truth.

“Tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Gentile”. The Jew first and also the Gentile. Why does Paul emphasize the Jew first? Who is he getting that from? He is getting it from the prophets, as he always did: the Lord saves Judah first, and Judah must rise first to teach the other tribes. That is why the gospel went to the Jews first and then to the Gentiles, as the book of Acts shows.

precepts.why: “The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first”: the Jew first. “That the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah”: that’s the rest of the tribes. Judah must rise first. This is where Paul gets “of the Jew first, and also of the Gentile.”

“And this is the blessing of Judah: and he said, Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him unto his people”. Bring him unto his people: bring him into Christ, and also bring him into the tribes. Judah must rise first to teach the other tribes. That is why Paul said in Romans 2:9, to the Jew first, then to the Gentile.

sense.text: This is read to show why Paul said in Romans 2:9 to the Jew first, then to the Gentile. “And Saul was consenting unto his death”: Stephen’s death, back in chapter 7. Stephen was killed, one of the seven deacons. “And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles.” The twelve remained in Jerusalem, but the seven, now six, were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria.

“And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip”: Philip, one of the six, because Stephen was the seventh. “Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert.”

“And, behold, a man of Ethiopia”: an African man, “an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure”, she put him over her treasure, “and had come to Jerusalem for to worship”. He came to Jerusalem to do what? To worship. An Ethiopian heathen, apparently, came to Jerusalem to worship. Read on and find out if he’s really an Ethiopian.

He “Was returning”, returning from worship at Jerusalem, “and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet.” He came from worshipping at Jerusalem with a Bible in his hand, reading the prophet. Interesting Ethiopian, this guy.

“Go near, and join thyself to this chariot”: go talk to him. Philip “heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?” Do you know what you’re reading right there? “How can I, except some man should guide me?” Can you teach me, I don’t know what I’m reading. “And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.”
