He was reading Isaiah 53: “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth: In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth.”

“Of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?” Is he referring to himself being killed, or somebody else? “Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.” He showed him that’s Christ right there; Isaiah 53 is referring to Christ. So Philip taught this man, and later in the chapter he baptized him.

precepts.why:
This took place during the persecution of Acts 8:1. “Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen”: the six, scattered when Stephen was killed. Acts 11 is a recap of chapter 10 and chapter 8. They “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.”

Wait a minute: then what was the Ethiopian Philip was talking to? They were preaching to the Jews only. He could have been an Ethiopian by country, but he was a Jew that came from Ethiopia. He worked for the Ethiopian queen guarding her treasure, he was able to leave from work and go worship, and as he was returning from worship Philip ran into him. He was a Jew, but he was called a heathen, called an Ethiopian, based upon where he was from. That’s why he came from worship.

Whenever you read of them teaching anyone before Cornelius, they were teaching Jews only. Christ, being the leader, set the precedent: he spoke to the woman at the well, Ephraim, a reminder that later on they were going to teach the northern kingdom, but for now they must teach the Jew first. Acts 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8: they are teaching Jews only and none else up until chapter 10 and Cornelius. Prior to that their ministry was to the circumcision only. That is the Jew first, and also the Gentile, of Romans 2:9.

sense.text: Remember: Jews only. “Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.” “But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death”: Christ raised Lazarus from the dead and they want to kill him again. That’s how evil they were.

“Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus”: by reason of Christ raising him from the dead, many of the Jews left them and started following Christ for his miracle.
“For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle”: they heard he had raised Lazarus from the dead.

“The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing?” We’re losing our followers. “Behold, the world is gone after him.” What world went after him in this chapter? The Jews. The Jews are the world; the Pharisees called their own people the world, based upon Isaiah 45:17. That’s the world he so loved.

“And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast”: came up to worship, during Passover. The ministry was to Jews only at this time; these were not white guys. They came up to worship God just like the Ethiopian in Acts 8 came to worship, because they were Israelites also.

Greek sources do not always distinguish between racial Greeks and Hellenized Asiatics, Hellenized Israelites, those of the east, because they were all doing the same thing. In the Hellenistic period, when the Greeks started to convert anybody into the Greek philosophy and culture, the term Greek ceased to be just Edomite Greeks and became a cultural concept, like American: originally for white folks, but no matter what you are, if you’re here you’re American. So the Greeks here were Israelites who adopted the culture and the language, Greek names and the Greek language, but still kept Mosaic law. The Greeks in John 12:20 were Israelites. It’s this clear cut.

“The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.” The same Greeks said, listen Philip, can we see Christ, can we meet him? “Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus”: the Greeks want to talk to you.

“And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.” “He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.” “If any man serve me, let him follow me”: he’s talking to the Greeks here. “And where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will my Father honour.”

“Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it”: the Father spoke. “The people therefore, that stood by”, the Greeks that came to talk to him, “said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him.” “Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.” Why would the voice of God come for heathens’ sakes? It didn’t. These Greeks are not heathens; these were Jews that were worshipping, and they heard the Father’s voice. The voice you heard came for your sakes, that you may believe in who I am.

“Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out”: they’re being cast out, they’re gonna fall. He ain’t talking to those white Greeks; he’s talking to his own people who are called Greeks.

“But contrariwise, when they saw that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter”: unto Peter, because they were teaching the Jews only. Then they realized the Lord sent Peter, first and foremost being the elder, and then the Lord passed the torch on to Paul and Barnabas to teach the northern kingdom afterwards. That was their ministry, and their ministry expanded after Acts 10.
“For he that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision, the same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles”.

“And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.” Paul goes unto our people scattered abroad, and the circumcision is the Jews: Judah and the northern kingdom.

“Behold, thou art called a Jew”: now we know who Paul’s writing to in Rome. That’s what was said earlier about “O man” that judges another: he was writing to the elders, the Jews of the synagogue in Rome, based upon Acts 28. Behold you Romans, you’re a Jew, “and restest in the law”, because they were elders of the law, “and makest thy boast of God”, keeping God’s laws. But they don’t have faith in Christ; that was what was missing.

Some read Romans 3 verse 1 and 2, not verse 3, then skip to verse 9 like those two work together: deceptive as hell. “What advantage then hath the Jew?” If the Jew has an advantage, then if you’re not a Jew you’re at a disadvantage; it’s just that clear. That’s Paul asking the question. “Or what profit is there of circumcision?” What profit is there of being circumcised?

“Much every way”: that part was skipped. There is every way an advantage to being a Jew and being of the circumcision. “Chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God”: unto the Israelites. Oracles means the words; unto us were committed the words of God, to keep them. So if we break God’s laws, or decide to break that commitment, we are held accountable for those actions.

Unto the Jews and Gentiles were committed the oracles of God, and they broke the laws: the Jews and Gentiles as Judah and Israel.

“What then? are we better than they?” Paul is referring to the Jews that disbelieved in Christ and were slandering him in his ministry. Shall their unbelief make God’s word void? God forbid. “No, in no wise”: not at all, because Paul was doing the same thing by murdering disciples. I was the same way as they were, I was in unbelief as well, until I was knocked off the horse and blind for three days. Even though their damnation is justified based on their disbelief, I am in no wise better than them.

“For we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”: proved out of what? Out of the law. To prove that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin you have to prove it out of the law and the prophets, that all nations are under the laws of Moses, because that’s what Christ died for: he died for those who broke the law of the old covenant.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”.
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus”. Who received justification? Let’s see where Paul got this from.

precepts.why: How do you prove anything regarding Jews and Gentiles being under sin? “And knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law”. To approve something means you have to prove it, and you prove it being instructed out of the law. So to prove that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin, you prove it out of the law and the prophets.

“In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified”. All the seed of Israel: justification is for the children of Israel. That’s what the prophets say. Where in the Old Testament does it say all nations to justification?

Who’s the all that have sinned? “Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law”: all Israel is under sin, “even by departing, that they might not obey thy voice; therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him.” That’s why all Israel is under sin.

All Israel transgressed the law: that’s Jews and Gentiles. In Daniel’s time this is the southern kingdom going into captivity; right before that the northern kingdom of Israel went into captivity under Assyria for breaking God’s laws. Then you got the southern kingdom being wicked as hell too, and God took them into captivity too. So all sinned, all.

sense.text: “I say the truth in Christ, I lie not”: Paul don’t lie.
“For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh”: according to my race, his kind, his flesh, his black dirty ungodly skin.

“Who are Israelites”: blood relatives. “To whom pertaineth the adoption”: Christ died on the cross adopting us back to the Father, and that belongs to Israel. “And the glory”: the glory belongs to Israel. “And the covenants”: the old and new covenants, in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, belong to Israel. “And the giving of the law”: the oracles committed unto them; the giving of the law belongs to the Israelites. “And the service of God”: being servants of God belongs to the Israelites. “And the promises”: passed down from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, they belong to the Israelites.

“Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came”: concerning the flesh of Paul, his race, Christ came. Christ came for the Israelites, not all nations. You can never get around Romans 9; Romans 9 alone destroys Christianity.

Mercy goes to Israel. “And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy”: the vessels of mercy are the children of Israel, “which he had afore prepared unto glory.” Afore means before; before where? In the Old Testament: that’s Isaiah 45:25, he would justify all the seed of Israel and they shall be glorified.

“Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles”. Who are the Jews and the Gentiles? Jews is Judah. Gentiles is the northern kingdom, because they were scattered and lost; and Judah, that returned from captivity in Babylon, for the most part remained scattered abroad too. Gentiles, or heathens, or strangers, or uncircumcision. You got to know the history: who was calling the ten tribes and saying you are not God’s people? When you read how Christ interacted with the Samaritan woman, and how the disciples perceived it, that alone should let you know.
Regarding the Jews and the Gentiles, “As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved.” That’s also in 1 Peter 2:10.

It gets worse for you Christians but it’s better for us: “And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God.”

“Esaias also crieth concerning Israel”: concerning who? Israel. I thought it was Jews and Gentiles in verse 24. Who’s the Jews and Gentiles in verse 24? Israel. “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved”: that’s Isaiah 10:22. So the Jews and Gentiles Paul is referring to are both kingdoms, Judah and Israel.

precepts.why: “Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel.” I will cause to cease the house of Israel: that’s the northern kingdom right there.

“And she conceived again, and bare a daughter. And God said unto him, Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.” I will utterly take the house of Israel away: they’ll be scattered, they’ll be lost.

“Then said God, Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” So what did Ephraim become at this point? Gentiles. You’re not my people, I’m not your God; you’re strangers from me, now you’re heathens, you’re Gentiles. That’s why Paul was quoting Hosea regarding the Jews and Gentiles: Judah and Ephraim.

Regarding Judah: “But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah”, I will have mercy on the Jews, “and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses”.

So the Jews believed that the northern kingdom was gone and cast off forever: you guys are heathens, the Lord ain’t doing nothing with you, only with Judah. Christ said no: he was sent to die to save both of you, to reunite both kingdoms. That was the confusion: the Jews were arrogant, believing that only those of the southern kingdom would be saved and not the other tribes. That was the arrogance Paul was getting them on about. You guys are just as wicked as the northern kingdom scattered abroad; you’re gonna die too if you don’t believe in me.

The Old Testament, and the New Testament, revolve around the restoring of the twelve tribes, not the restoring of a heathen and Israelite coalition. That ain’t biblical; that’s democracy, that’s Hellenism, Christian Hellenism.

“Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered”: that’s Revelation 7:9, a number no man could number. “And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.” That’s Romans 9:24-25.

“Then shall the children of Judah”, the Jews, “and the children of Israel”, the Gentiles, “be gathered together”: come back, grafted in again, Romans 11. “And appoint themselves one head”: Christ. “And they shall come up out of the land: for great shall be the day of Jezreel.” Great shall be the deliverance.

“And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.” This is what Paul quotes in Romans 9:25, and it is the same in 1 Peter 2:10.

“But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him”. Peter talked to the strangers that are scattered abroad: the Israelite strangers, or Gentiles, or heathen, or uncircumcision, “who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light”.

“Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” Peter is quoting Hosea regarding Ephraim. Peter was writing to the Israelites scattered abroad, and he confirms that Paul was talking to the same people.

“O Lord our God, thou hast dealt with us after all thy goodness, and according to all that great mercy of thine, As thou spakest by thy servant Moses in the day when thou didst command him to write the law before the children of Israel, saying, If ye will not hear my voice, surely this very great multitude shall be turned into a small number among the nations, where I will scatter them.” God knew that Israel would get split and there’d be Jews and Gentiles, Judah and Ephraim, “because it is a stiffnecked people”.

“But in the land of their captivities they shall remember themselves”: in the valley of the shadow of death and the places of darkness where we’re living at now. We’re going to begin to remember who we are. That’s happening now, and it’s scaring people to the point where they refuse to come out and talk to us, but that’s okay, because it was prophesied that we were going to remember ourselves and learn who we are.

“And they shall praise me in the land of their captivity”: we’re doing that right now. “And think upon my name”: we’re going to think upon this Bible, his word. “For they shall remember the way of their fathers”: that means they’re a race of people, not a spirit, not a spiritual church. Remember themselves means remember who we are: it was lost and now it’s being found.

“And I will bring them again into the land which I promised with an oath unto their fathers”, their race, “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they shall be lords of it”: lords of it and of everybody else. “And I will make an everlasting covenant with them to be their God, and they shall be my people: and I will no more drive my people of Israel out of the land that I have given them.”
